summary: Specifies how members of the IAB and IESG are selected, confirmed and recalled, including the operation of nominating and recall committees. It compiles the process as known at the time. It is a Best Current Practice and was replaced by RFC 3777.

plainLanguage.summary: It is the rule book for picking and replacing the leaders of the Internet standards groups, like school election rules.

questions: how are iab and iesg members selected
how many people are on the nominating committee
how can an iesg member be recalled
subtitle: The rulebook for how the Internet's standards leaders are picked, confirmed and, if needed, recalled.

tldr.problem: The IETF needed a written, self-consistent process for choosing members of the IAB and IESG, which had until then relied partly on oral tradition passed between committee chairs.
tldr.mechanism: A nominating committee of randomly chosen volunteers reviews about half of the open positions each year and presents one candidate per position to a confirming body, using an advise and consent model. A separate recall committee, built the same way, can remove a sitting member.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2727 was a revision of RFC 2282 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 3777, so it describes the process as of February 2000, not the current one.

facts.label: Volunteer eligibility
facts.value: Attended at least 2 of the last 3 IETF meetings

today: RFC 2727 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 10) that was obsoleted by RFC 3777, so it no longer describes the current process. It had itself replaced RFC 2282.

sections.title: What the Process Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2727 specifies the process by which members of the IAB and IESG are selected, confirmed and recalled. It revises and supersedes RFC 2282 and is a compilation of the process as it was known when it was published. The rules take effect immediately when approved, even if this document has not yet been revised.

Two assumptions carry over: the IRTF and IRSG are not part of the process, and the organization or re-organization of the IESG is not part of it either. Time frames are measured from the First IETF meeting of the calendar year, and assume the IETF meets at least once a year.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the instruction sheet for choosing the grown-ups who steer the Internet's standards groups. It also says how to replace one who is not doing a good job.

sections.title: General Rules for Selection and Confirmation
sections.content:
The nominating committee reviews the open IESG and IAB positions and either nominates the incumbent or recruits a better candidate. It is told which positions to review; it does not choose them, and it does not confirm its own candidates. Incumbents must tell the committee if they do not want to be nominated.

The annual process should finish within 3 months, ending one month before the Friday of the week before the First IETF and starting 4 months before it. About one-half of the IESG and IAB positions are reviewed each year, and confirmed candidates are expected to serve at least a 2 year term. The committee may assign longer terms to some positions so that reviews stay evenly spread. Terms start and end at the First IETF meeting, normally when the sitting member's term ends on the last day of the meeting.

Mid-term vacancies follow the same rules with four changes: the most recent committee is reconvened, the process should finish within 1 month, the confirming body has two weeks to reject a candidate (otherwise the candidate is taken as confirmed), and the term is the remainder of the open term, or the remainder plus a 2 year term if less than one year is left.

All deliberations and supporting information about nominees, candidates and confirmed candidates are confidential.
sections.plainLanguage: Every year about half of the leader jobs come up for a fresh look, so there is never a moment when everyone changes at once. Everything said about the people being considered stays secret.

sections.title: Advise and Consent
sections.content:
Unless stated otherwise, the process uses an advise and consent model. The IETF Executive Director advises the nominating committee which positions to review. The committee selects candidates and advises the confirming bodies. The sitting IAB members review the IESG candidates, and the Internet Society Board of Trustees reviews the IAB candidates. Each can consent to some, all or none.

If some or none are confirmed, the nominating committee must reconvene to pick alternates for the rejected candidates, without exceeding its maximum time allotment. The confirming bodies choose their own mechanism, but at least one-half of the sitting members must agree to confirm or reject each nominee. A formal vote, informal email consensus, or the body's usual way of doing business are all acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee suggests a name, and a second group has to say yes. If they say no, the committee has to come back with another name.

sections.title: Building and Running the Nominating Committee
sections.content:
The committee has at least a non-voting Chair, 10 voting volunteers and 3 non-voting liaisons. The Internet Society President appoints the Chair, who publishes the list of open positions and asks for volunteers. To volunteer, a person must have attended at least 2 of the last 3 IETF meetings. Internet Society trustees and sitting IAB and IESG members may not volunteer.

The Chair randomly selects the 10 voting members from the announced pool using a method that can be independently verified as fair and unbiased. The method must announce the list of names and the algorithm in advance, and the output must depend on random data not known at that time. Sitting IAB and IESG members each appoint a liaison, and the prior year's Chair, or a designee, is also a non-voting liaison.

In operation, the Chair must publish milestones, including at least a call for nominations, and set up a voting mechanism. A quorum is at least 7 voting members. Anyone in the IETF community may nominate anyone, including themselves. Committee members cannot be nominees, and people recalled from the IESG or IAB in the previous two years cannot be nominees either. Nominees must consent in writing, and the committee presents a single candidate per position with a testament of how that person meets the qualifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee members are drawn by lot, like a jury, so nobody can rig who is picked. Each person has to say yes before they can be put forward.

sections.title: Recalling a Sitting Member
sections.content:
Anyone may ask for the recall of a sitting IAB or IESG member, at any time, with a written request and justification sent to the Internet Society President. The President appoints a Recall Committee Chair but must not evaluate the request: judging the behavior of its leaders is explicitly the IETF community's job.

The recall committee is created and run under the nominating committee's rules, except that neither the person being investigated nor the requester may be a member, and there is no confirmation step. It investigates, which must include a written statement from the member and consultation with third parties, and votes. A 3/4 majority of those voting is needed to recall, and the open position is then filled under the mid-term vacancy rules.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone thinks a leader is doing a poor job, a fresh group is drawn by lot to look into it. The leader gets to tell their side, and a big majority must agree before they are removed.

sections.title: Confidentiality and Changes from RFC 2282
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is about privacy: any selection, confirmation or recall process investigates the qualifications and activities of candidates, which may reveal confidential or private information. Everyone who takes part is responsible for keeping confidential anything not explicitly marked as suitable for public release.

The substantive changes from RFC 2282 include switching the time reference from the "Spring IETF" to the "First IETF", allowing sitting and incoming terms to overlap during that meeting, letting past committee members advise the current one, clarifying advisors and liaisons, adding a reference to a fair random selection method, and making clear that responsibility rests with the committee as a whole rather than the Chair.
sections.plainLanguage: People checking on candidates learn private things, so everyone involved has to keep quiet about them. The rules were also tidied up a bit from the older version.
